problems.title: Reading constraints
problems.statement: Pick the largest complexity that fits in about a second (≈10⁸ simple operations).
problems.solution: 2ⁿ·n at n = 20 is 2·10⁷; n² at 5,000 is 2.5·10⁷; n log n at 10⁶ is 2·10⁷; at 10¹⁸ only logarithmic (or constant) work fits.

problems.title: Operation counts

parts.prompt: n = 10⁵, O(n log₂ n): operations (millions, to 1 decimal)?

problems.solution: 10¹⁰ operations, about 100 s: far too slow. n log n is about 1.7 million: milliseconds.

problems.title: Hidden costs
problems.statement: A Python loop over n = 10⁵ items does result = result + s[i] (string concatenation, copying the whole string each time).

options: Append to a list and ''.join at the end

hints: Each concatenation copies the current length.
problems.solution: 1 + 2 + … + n ≈ n²/2 = 5·10⁹ characters: quadratic. Building a list and joining once is linear.

problems.title: Recurrences
hints: Draw the recursion tree: work per level × levels.
problems.solution: Merge sort; binary search; naive Fibonacci-style branching; a loop that shrinks by one each time (selection sort).

problems.title: Amortised
problems.statement: A dynamic array starts with capacity 1 and doubles when full. Append n = 1,024 elements.

parts.prompt: Element copies done by all the resizes?

problems.solution: 1 + 2 + … + 512 = 1,023 copies; with the 1,024 writes, about 2 operations per append: O(1) amortised.

problems.title: A nested loop that's linear
problems.statement: j = 0; for i in range(n): while j < n and cond(i, j): j += 1

parts.prompt: Maximum total executions of j += 1 over the whole run, for n = 1000?

problems.solution: j only increases and stops at n, so the inner body runs at most n times in total: O(n). This is the sliding-window argument.

problems.title: Space
problems.statement: Recursive DFS on a path-shaped tree of n = 10⁵ nodes.

options: RecursionError (default limit about 1000) or stack overflow; use an explicit stack

problems.solution: Depth n: O(n) stack space, and Python's default recursion limit is about 1,000. Use an explicit stack, or raise the limit carefully.

problems.title: Expected versus worst
problems.statement: A hash map with adversarially chosen keys that all collide.

parts.prompt: Cost of n insertions in the worst case?

hints: Each insertion scans a chain of the colliding keys.
problems.solution: O(n²) worst case, O(n) expected. Say "expected O(1) per operation"; the alternative with guarantees is a balanced tree, O(log n).

problems.title: Lower bounds

options: Any algorithm must read all n inputs: Ω(n)
Comparison sorting needs Ω(n log n) comparisons
Output of size k needs Ω(k) time

problems.solution: The first three are standard; reaching them means you can stop and say so.

problems.title: Choosing by constraints
problems.statement: Find the number of pairs (i < j) with a[i] + a[j] ≤ T, n ≤ 2·10⁵.

options: Sort, then two pointers or binary search: O(n log n)

parts.prompt: Pairs examined by all-pairs for n = 2·10⁵ (billions, 1 decimal)?

problems.solution: About 20.0 billion pairs: too many. After sorting, for each i the valid j form a prefix: two pointers count them in O(n) after the O(n log n) sort.
